purpose:
This report presents the Car
Park Signage Plan for Thanet, developed following an independent
review by Ethos. The plan establishes a district-wide strategy to
replace limited, inconsistent directional signage with a coherent
three-tier hierarchy (strategic, arterial, and local routes),
introduces spatial zoning (Seafront, Town Centre, and Harbour
zones) with revised, intuitive car park naming conventions, and
identifies locations for static and Variable Message Signs (VMS)
across the district.
content:
This report presents the Car
Park Signage Plan for Thanet, developed following an independent
review by Ethos. The plan establishes a district-wide strategy to
replace limited, inconsistent directional signage with a coherent
three-tier hierarchy (strategic, arterial, and local routes),
introduces spatial zoning (Seafront, Town Centre, and Harbour
zones) with revised, intuitive car park naming conventions, and
identifies locations for static and Variable Message Signs (VMS)
across the district.

Cabinet agreed the following
recommendations:
 
1. 
That the Car Park Signage Plan be adopted and that
the officers engage councillors in change of car park names prior
to implementation.

Adoption and implementation of
the plan will provide clear, consistent directional signage for
residents, visitors, and businesses across Thanet. This will reduce
circulating traffic, ease congestion, prevent overspill parking on
residential streets, support town centre regeneration, and improve
the overall arrival experience for visitors to the
district.

Cabinet considered the
alternative option of not adopting and implementing the Car Park
Signage Plan. This was rejected because maintaining the status quo
would fail to resolve existing directional inconsistencies, would
not address visitor frustration or town centre congestion, and
would offer no strategic improvements for the district.

purpose:
This report seeks approval to
proceed with the redevelopment, subject to a successful application
for Homes England grant for social rent. The detailed cost of the
redevelopment is £3,330,000 inclusive of fees and expenses,
with construction costs calculated as £2,737,167.
content:
This report seeks approval to
proceed with the redevelopment, subject to a successful application
for Homes England grant for social rent. The detailed cost of the
redevelopment is £3,330,000 inclusive of fees and expenses,
with construction costs calculated as £2,737,167.

Cabinet agreed the
following:
 
1. 
To approve the spend of £3,330,000 in the HRA
to redevelop the Edgar Road building to provide 10 permanent homes
for households on the housing register;
 
2. 
To set a social rent for the homes, making them
genuinely affordable and satisfying Homes England’s 2026-2036
eligibility criteria;
 
3. 
To agree that the new homes are let in accordance
with the council’s approved allocations policy, subject to an
approved local letting plan.

The scheme brings the building
back into use, in line with the aspirations for it when it was
acquired using LiveMargate funding back in 2023. It also provides
10 much-needed homes for households on the housing register.
Setting social rent levels means the homes are genuinely affordable
and the scheme accesses Homes England grant funding.

Option 1 - mothball the site -
effectively mark the scheme for now - though costs of over
£55,000 would be incurred to do this.
 
Option 2 - disposal - this is
discounted as no private developer will likely take the site on
with high levels of expenditure involved - the council would also
have to return the LiveMargate funds that acquired the
site.
 
Option 3 - higher density
scheme - this is not possible due to the rules on 1-bedroom homes
in the Cliftonville area.
 
Option 4 - lower quality scheme
- discounted as it would not be in line with corporate plan goals
of delivering homes with reduced carbon.

purpose:
To provide the Cabinet with two
reports that are required by regulation to be published on the
Council’s website. The reports are:
 
· 
Tenant and Leaseholder Services Annual Report
2024/25;
 
· 
Annual Complaints Performance and Service
Improvement Report 2024/25.
content:
To provide the Cabinet with two
reports that are required by regulation to be published on the
Council’s website. The reports are:
 
· 
Tenant and Leaseholder Services Annual Report
2024/25;
 
· 
Annual Complaints Performance and Service
Improvement Report 2024/25.

Cabinet agreed the following,
to:
 
1. 
Approve the Tenant and Leaseholder Services Annual
Report 2025/26;
 
2.  Approve the Complaints Performance and
Service Improvement Report 2025/26.

The publishing of the two
reports is recommended for the following reasons:
 
· 
The Regulator for Social Housing tells us we must
provide timely and relevant information to support the effective
scrutiny by tenants of their landlords’ performance and such
provision must include the publication of an annual report. The
annual report should include information on repairs and maintenance
budgets.
 
· 
The Social Housing Regulation Act 2023 has
strengthened the powers of the Housing Ombudsman. Housing providers
must show compliance with the Housing Ombudsman's complaint
handling code. One of the requirements is to publish an Annual
Complaints Performance and Service Improvement Report.

The option to reject or amend
the proposed reports was rejected. These reports are supported by
Cabinet and are a regulatory requirement.

purpose:
The Cabinet considered a report
recommending the leasehold disposal of three surplus property
assets: Nethercourt Touring Park, Ramsgate; Land adjacent to
Millies Bar & Restaurant, Westgate and the Palm Bay Avenue
shelter, Palm Bay, Margate. The disposal of surplus assets is
crucial in generating capital receipts and income, which is
essential for funding the council’s approved Capital
Programme as set out in the Medium Term Financial Plan.
content:
The Cabinet considered a report
recommending the leasehold disposal of three surplus property
assets: Nethercourt Touring Park, Ramsgate; Land adjacent to
Millies Bar & Restaurant, Westgate and the Palm Bay Avenue
shelter, Palm Bay, Margate. The disposal of surplus assets is
crucial in generating capital receipts and income, which is
essential for funding the council’s approved Capital
Programme as set out in the Medium Term Financial Plan.

Cabinet agreed the following
recommendations, to:
 
1. 
Approve the leasehold disposal of Nethercourt
Touring Park, Ramsgate;
 
2.  Approve the asset disposal of Land adjacent
to Millies Bar & Restaurant, Westgate;
 
3. 
Approve the leasehold disposal of the Palm Bay
Avenue Shelter, Margate.

The assets have been identified
surplus to council requirements. There is cost and risk to the
council associated with retaining these properties on a long term
basis. Their leasehold disposals will generate much-needed rental
income that can be utilised elsewhere in the council’s
retained portfolio or statutory services.

The options to retain the
assets and repurpose them were all rejected because they would be
financially imprudent, fail to generate the necessary funds for the
council, and would not address the financial or safety risks
associated with retaining the properties on a long term
basis.

purpose:
This report provides Cabinet
with the new Vessel Disposal Policy for consideration and adoption.
The policy establishes an updated, legally sound procedure for the
arrest, detention, and disposal of vessels with outstanding harbour
dues at the Port of Ramsgate. The policy confirms the use of
statutory powers available under Sections 44 and 45 of the
Harbours, Docks and Piers Clauses Act 1847.
content:
This report provides Cabinet
with the new Vessel Disposal Policy for consideration and adoption.
The policy establishes an updated, legally sound procedure for the
arrest, detention, and disposal of vessels with outstanding harbour
dues at the Port of Ramsgate. The policy confirms the use of
statutory powers available under Sections 44 and 45 of the
Harbours, Docks and Piers Clauses Act 1847.

Cabinet agreed the
following:
 
1. 
To adopt the Vessel Disposal Policy presented as
Annex 1 to the Cabinet report, with effect from 7 September
2026.

To establish an efficient,
legally robust framework for recovering unpaid harbour dues and
managing seized vessels. Transitioning to Sections 44 and 45 of the
Harbours, Docks and Piers Clauses Act 1847 enables the Council to
sell distrained vessels at market value rather than at discounted
public auction rates. This maximises financial recovery for the
Council and reduces the recurrence of abandoned vessels.

Cabinet considered maintaining
the status quo by continuing to rely on current vessel disposal
processes under Section 41 of the Council’s general disposal
policy. This option was rejected because existing procedures have
proven ineffective, frequently leading to vessels selling
significantly below market value and being subsequently
re-abandoned, which forces the Council to repeatedly restart debt
recovery proceedings.

purpose:
This report presents the
proposal to formally adopt the Thanet District Council Tenancy
Strategy and Tenant Management Policy. Previously updated in 2022,
the documents have been reviewed and revised to ensure compliance
with recent legislative changes and align with current social and
housing data to address local needs.
 
Local Authorities are mandated
by the Localism Act 2011 to publish a Tenancy Strategy. This
strategy provides guidance to Registered Providers of Social
Housing (RP’s) regarding their tenancy management policies
and other such policies and guidelines that affect their
tenants.
 
The Tenant Management Policy is
required by all social landlords and should regard the contents of
the Tenancy Strategy. The policy outlines what tenancy flexibility
can be offered, how tenancies are managed, how tenancies are ended
and criteria for tenancy succession.
 
While both the Tenancy Strategy
and Tenant Management Policy have their own defined purpose, there
is significant overlap between the two documents. Therefore, it was
judged that both should be brought before Cabinet together as the
updates and refresh are more often relevant to both
documents.

Strategy and Tenant Management Policy. Previously updated in 2022,

housing data to address local needs.

Cabinet agreed the following,
to:
 

Approve the draft
Tenancy Strategy and Tenant Management Policy for
adoption.


It is a statutory requirement

purpose:
This report provides the
2026/27 budget monitor for General Fund revenue and capital
forecasts against budget, as well as the Housing Revenue Account to
the 30 June 2026. This report also details work underway to address
structural pressures.
content:
This report provides the
2026/27 budget monitor for General Fund revenue and capital
forecasts against budget, as well as the Housing Revenue Account to
the 30 June 2026. This report also details work underway to address
structural pressures.

Cabinet agreed the following,
to:
 
1. 
Approve a one-off General Fund revenue virement
amounting to £269,035 for the 2026/27 financial year, as set
out in Annex 4 (to the Cabinet report). This comprises
£188,000 assigned specifically to support cleansing services
in 2026/27, with the remaining £81,000 retained within
contingency;
 
2. 
Agree to the following capital programme budget
changes:
 
(i)  Scheme reprofiling as set out in section 9.3 and
Annex 1 to the report.
(ii) Budget
adjustments as set out in section 9.5 and Annex 1 to the
report.
 
3. 
To agree a virement of £190k within the
2026/27 HRA revenue budget to provide additional funding for
completing the programme of the stock condition surveys, to be
funded from the forecast underspend from the Waking
Watch.

The report provides Cabinet
with a view on the 2026/27 forecast outturn for General Fund
revenue and capital, as well as the Housing Revenue Account. The
decisions are required to approve necessary budget adjustments for
revenue as well as to the Capital Programme and to recommend
approvals to Council where appropriate to ensure finances continue
to be sound and the Council meets its duty to monitor
spending.

Cabinet considered not
approving the budget variations or adjustments. This was rejected
because insufficient budget would be available for the proposed
usage detailed in the report. Consequently, those schemes and
initiatives would either need to be aborted or officers would need
to return to Cabinet with alternative recommendations at a later
date.

purpose:
Thanet District Council has
developed the Health in All Policies (HiAP) to capture the work of
the council in a draft Action Plan and incorporate Health Equity
considerations into corporate report templates for key decisions.
The HiAP provides a coordinated framework that brings together
actions already being delivered across the council and its
partners.
content:
Thanet District Council has
developed the Health in All Policies (HiAP) to capture the work of
the council in a draft Action Plan and incorporate Health Equity
considerations into corporate report templates for key decisions.
The HiAP provides a coordinated framework that brings together
actions already being delivered across the council and its
partners.

Cabinet agreed the following,
to:
 
1. 
Approve the adoption and implementation of the
Health in All Policies (2026);
 
2. 
Agree that the provisions of the HiAP be incorporated into other council strategies,
as appropriate;
 
3. 
Support the continued cross-service and partnership
approach to improving health and reducing health inequalities in
the district; and note Thanet’s status as an ‘Anchor
Organisation’ within the Kent Marmot Coastal
Region.

The adoption of the HiAP will
give health equity a higher priority and ensure every corporate
decision considers these implications for Thanet residents: through
the health screening tool, placing health on an equal reporting
footing with statutory equality and net-zero obligations. This
approach reflects best practice, where adoption of the policy will
demonstrate the council’s commitment to health improvement,
reducing inequalities, and sustainable growth.

Alternative 1 - Adopt the
Health in All Policies (HiAP) 2026, with amendments. The policy
could be amended to be more or less prescriptive and include
different requirements. This policy has been drafted to meet
current legislation and guidance requirements.
 
Alternative 2 - Not to adopt
the Health in All Policies (HiAP) 2026, as this is not considered a
priority for the council. This option is not recommended given the
council’s corporate plan commitments to the health of its
residents. This would also reduce emerging opportunities provided
by public health partners in using the Kent Marmot Coastal Region
framework to aid in effective decision making and securing
appropriate funding to reduce health inequalities in
Thanet.

purpose:
To seek Cabinet’s
authority to consult on the proposed “Public Spaces
Protection Order (Dog Control) 2026” to be agreed for a
period of three years; with an amendment for additional dog control
measures between Cold Harbour and Plum Pudding.
content:
To seek Cabinet’s
authority to consult on the proposed “Public Spaces
Protection Order (Dog Control) 2026” to be agreed for a
period of three years; with an amendment for additional dog control
measures between Cold Harbour and Plum Pudding.

Cabinet agreed the
following:
 
1. 
To consult on the proposed PSPO in accordance with
the statutory requirements, that is to say to consult with the
local chief officer of police; the police and crime commissioner;
owners or occupiers of land within the proposed affected area,
appropriate community representatives and the relevant local parish
councils.

There is a statutory
requirement for public consultation under Section 72(16) of the
Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014, and to
conscientiously consider the results before implementing a PSPO.
This report is seeking Cabinet’s authority to consult, after
first having considered, the evidence base for the proposed order.
Once the results of consultation have been carefully considered by
officers, a further report will be presented to Cabinet to consider
whether the PSPO should be made. The Public Space Protection Order
for Dog Control was originally approved in October 2017 and was
amended and extended in both October 2020 and October 2023, for
three years on each occasion, in accordance with the provisions of
the Antisocial Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act 2014. Public Space
Protection Orders are valid for 3 years following approval. 
The issuing of the Dog PSPO is necessary to prevent anti-social
activity recurring. This report is requesting a PSPO for dog
control for 3 years in accordance with Section 60 of the Act.
Public consultation is required for this renewal under Section
72(16) of the Anti-social Behaviour, Crime and Policing Act
2014.

Alternative 1 - Not to consult
on the PSPO for Dog Control, as this is not considered a priority
for the council. Cabinet could take the view that it does not wish
to progress the proposed new PSPO at Annex 1 to the Cabinet report.
This was not recommended as it is clear that the issues the order
seeks to address are significant across the proposed restricted
areas, that they are having a detrimental impact on the local
community and that education alone is not completely effective in
addressing these issues without a graduated enforcement
approach.

purpose:
Thanet District Council has
developed a Tackling Poverty Strategy to bring together internal
and external partners and create a Tackling Poverty Network Group
to monitor actions across a range of poverty indicators to address
the causes and effects of deprivation in Thanet.
content:
Thanet District Council has
developed a Tackling Poverty Strategy to bring together internal
and external partners and create a Tackling Poverty Network Group
to monitor actions across a range of poverty indicators to address
the causes and effects of deprivation in Thanet.

Cabinet agreed the
following:
 

The adoption of the
Tackling Poverty Strategy (2026);

 
2. 
That the provisions of the Tackling Poverty Strategy
be incorporated into other council policies, including Health in
All Policy (HiAP), as
appropriate.

The 2025 Indices of Deprivation
rank Thanet wards within the bottom 10% of most deprived local
authority districts in England. Poverty in the district is
multidimensional, evidenced by significant health inequalities,
such as a three-year lower male life expectancy compared to the
South East average, 26.3% of children in Thanet living in relative
low-income families, and 14% of households facing fuel poverty.
Thanet faces unique socio-economic challenges as a coastal
community, ranking 26th most deprived out of 296 local authorities
in England. This strategy aligns existing efforts with new
frameworks like the UK’s first Marmot Coastal Region
initiative to tackle the social determinants of health.

Alternative 1 - Adopt the
Tackling Poverty Strategy 2026, with amendments. This policy has
been drafted to meet current legislation and guidance
requirements. 
 
Alternative 2 - Not to adopt
the Tackling Poverty Strategy, as this is not considered a priority
for the council. This option is not recommended given the
council’s Corporate Plan 2024-2028 commitments to community
and the health equity of residents.

decision_maker: Director of Corporate Services & S151 Officer
purpose:
This decision is written to
provide context around partial exemption and why this option is
required. The option to tax option is an essential element of the
Councils Tax Planning and to secure best value for the
Council.
 
We have looked at both the
current 7 year average which sits at 2.85% and the in year position which is projected at circa 3% to
decide on whether ‘not opting to tax’ would see us
breach our partial exemption limit.
 
The combined estimated
£12.8m spend on these projects, Theatre Royal £6mil,
Clock House £4.4m, Skatepark £1.3m and Walpole
£1.1m in isolation would see us breach partial exemption in
year if we didn’t opt to tax, it would also leave little or
no headroom based on the 7 year average.
 
The financial impact of the
breach would result in the council being unable to reclaim VAT on
the £12.8m spend and also typically have to repay all the VAT
related to exempt supplies previously recovered.
 
The solution to this, from the
Council's perspective, is to "opt to tax" the land for each of the
projects.  This will result in any
‘rent’ (may include insurance rent) charges (both the
"actual" charges and the invoices raised by the Council in respect
of any barter arrangements) being subject to VAT.
 
As indicated above, based on
current projections the headroom of 5% would be exceeded by 24.43%
in year if the option is not taken, this would see our projected
up-and-coming period stay in excess of 6.8%, assuming that all
other spend returns to ‘base’ i.e. no significant
spend.
 
Consequences of breaching the
partial exemption limit in a financial year are severe: if the
limit is exceeded (and cannot be contained under the seven-year
average), the authority cannot recover any VAT related to its
exempt supplies for that financial year, which can have significant
financial implications.
 
 
VAT
Analysis - from our Tax Advisors
 
Theatre Royal
To be certain of safeguarding
the VAT recovery position, the Council might consider opting to tax
the theatre. By making a taxable supply of the lease, the Council
will be able to recover all of the VAT on the refurbishment of the
property.
 
If the third party is an
"eligible body" (as defined in section 4 of HMRC notice 701/47),
qualifying admission charges will be VAT-exempt. This would reduce
their ability to recover VAT incurred on their expenditure -
including payments under the lease, should the Council opt to tax.
This might affect the level of rent that the third party could
afford to pay.
The third party operator would
naturally incur VAT on the lease from the Council. If they are VAT
registered and provided they are making taxable supplies, they
should be able to recover the VAT charged on the lease. If however,
they are partly exempt, they may not be able to deduct all VAT
charged and they would need to run any VAT charged on the lease
through their own partial exemption calculation to determine
whether they can recover it fully.
 
Clock
House
As with the other projects, the
risk is partial exemption. I would suggest that the Council
considers opting to tax the site (will cover both the museum
building and café extension). The café operator is
likely to be VAT registered and so able to recover the VAT charged
on rent.  By default, admission charges
by the Council to an in-house run museum would be standard
rated.  There is a “cultural
exemption” that Councils can seek, which would make the
admission charges VAT-exempt – however I would suggest that
the Council does not do so, as any increase in admission income
would be more than outweighed by the cost of a partial exemption
breach.
 
 
Walpole Bay Beach Facilities
You need to start by
considering the VAT treatment of the activities following the
construction. Letting out a cafe would likely be VAT-exempt unless
you opt to tax. The "community container" is likely to be the same
- although if it is supplied specifically for storage purposes,
rents would likely be taxable regardless of any option to
tax.  If the toilets/showers are
operated by the Council, this element will be non-business.
Although there is a non-business element to the project, the
cafe/community facility could still result in a significant
proportion of the build cost needing to be included in the partial
exemption calculation if the Council does not opt to tax. Opting to
tax would require VAT to be added to rents - this might be
recoverable by the cafe operator and community facility hirers if
they are VAT registered, but it is quite likely that some smaller
groups will not be.
 
Skatepark
Similarly, you need to assess
the VAT treatment of operating income. Will the skatepark itself be
operated by the Council - or will it be let to an operator? I
assume that the commercial kiosk will be a lease/letting,
generating income which will be VAT-exempt unless the Council opts
to tax. As with Walpole Bay, a public toilet operated by the
Council is a non-business activity. Once you have assessed the
proportion of intended exempt activity, determine the effect on
partial exemption, and opt to tax if the de minimis is at
risk.
 
 
Option To Tax is generally irrevocable for 20 years.
Once a property has been opted,
then (apart from a brief "cooling off" period) it cannot normally
be revoked for at least 20 years. However, it currently seems
probable that LGR proposals will result in the creation of a new
unitary authority, which will take on the activities of the
Council, other neighbouring authorities and the relevant parts of
the County. This new authority will likely have a new VAT
registration number. In previous LGR exercises, HMRC have taken the
view that options to tax made by the authorities which cease to
exist under LGR will lapse, and it will be for the successor
authority to decide whether or not it wishes to opt to tax specific
sites.  Depending upon both the stage of
the works and the successor authority's forecast of its partial
exemption position, it might decide that it does not need to opt to
tax.

probable that LGR proposals will result in the creation of a new
unitary authority, which will take on the activities of the
Council, other neighbouring authorities and the relevant parts of
the County. This new authority will likely have a new VAT
registration number. In previous LGR exercises, HMRC have taken the
view that options to tax made by the authorities which cease to
exist under LGR will lapse, and it will be for the successor
authority to decide whether or not it wishes to opt to tax specific
sites.  Depending upon both the stage of
the works and the successor authority's forecast of its partial
exemption position, it might decide that it does not need to opt to
tax.

Opt to tax the Theatre Royal,
Clock House, Walpole Beach Facilities and Skatepark with effect
from 23/07/26 as these regeneration projects progress to lease
stages.

Without an option to tax, the
leases to the tenants for the four projects would be VAT-exempt,
and any VAT chargeable in connection to the works would need
inclusion within the Council’s partial exemption
calculation.
 
This would cause a partial
exemption issue - in that the amount of input tax incurred by the
Council on the charges from the four Projects would result in a
breach of the Council's 5% de minimis limit.
 
Therefore, to avoid the Council
having to payback any previously reclaimed VAT an option to tax is
required to reduce the Council’s financial risk
exposure.
 
 
Background Information
This decision is written to
provide context around partial exemption and why this option is
required. The option to tax option is an essential element of the
Councils Tax Planning and to secure best value for the
Council.
 
We have looked at both the
current 7 year average which sits at
2.85% and the in year position which is
projected at circa 3% to decide on whether ‘not opting to
tax’ would see us breach our partial exemption
limit.
 
The combined estimated
£12.8m spend on these projects, Theatre Royal £6mil,
Clock House £4.4m, Skatepark £1.3m and Walpole
£1.1m in isolation would see us breach partial exemption in
year if we didn’t opt to tax, it would also leave little or
no headroom based on the 7 year
average.
 
The financial impact of the
breach would result in the council being unable to reclaim VAT on
the £12.8m spend and also typically have to repay all the VAT
related to exempt supplies previously recovered.
 
The solution to this, from the
Council's perspective, is to "opt to tax" the land for each of the
projects. This will result in any ‘rent’ (may include
insurance rent) charges (both the "actual" charges and the invoices
raised by the Council in respect of any barter arrangements) being
subject to VAT.
 
As indicated above, based on
current projections the headroom of 5% would be exceeded by 24.43%
in year if the option is not taken, this would see our projected
up-and-coming period stay in excess of 6.8%, assuming that all
other spend returns to ‘base’ i.e. no significant spend.
 
Consequences of breaching the
partial exemption limit in a financial year are severe: if the
limit is exceeded (and cannot be contained under the seven-year
average), the authority cannot recover any VAT related to its
exempt supplies for that financial year, which can have significant
financial implications.
 
 
VAT
Analysis - from our Tax Advisors
 
Theatre Royal
To be certain of safeguarding
the VAT recovery position, the Council might consider opting to tax
the theatre. By making a taxable supply of the lease, the Council
will be able to recover all of the VAT on the refurbishment of the
property.
 
If the third party is an
"eligible body" (as defined in section 4 of HMRC notice 701/47),
qualifying admission charges will be VAT-exempt. This would reduce
their ability to recover VAT incurred on their expenditure -
including payments under the lease, should the Council opt to tax.
This might affect the level of rent that the third party could
afford to pay.
 
The third
party operator would naturally incur VAT on the lease from
the Council. If they are VAT registered and provided they are making taxable supplies, they
should be able to recover the VAT charged on the lease.
If however, they are partly exempt, they
may not be able to deduct all VAT charged and they would need to
run any VAT charged on the lease through their own partial
exemption calculation to determine whether they can recover it
fully.
 
Clock House
As with the other projects, the
risk is partial exemption. I would suggest that the Council
considers opting to tax the site (will cover both the museum
building and café extension). The café operator is
likely to be VAT registered and so able to recover the VAT charged
on rent. By default, admission charges by the Council to an
in-house run museum would be standard rated. There is a
“cultural exemption” that Councils can seek, which
would make the admission charges VAT-exempt – however I would
suggest that the Council does not do so, as any increase in
admission income would be more than outweighed by the cost of a
partial exemption breach.
 
Walpole Bay Beach
Facilities
You need to start by
considering the VAT treatment of the activities following the
construction. Letting out a cafe would likely be VAT-exempt unless
you opt to tax. The "community container" is likely to be the same
- although if it is supplied specifically for storage purposes,
rents would likely be taxable regardless of any option to tax. If
the toilets/showers are operated by the Council, this element will
be non-business. Although there is a non-business element to the
project, the cafe/community facility could still result in a
significant proportion of the build cost needing to be included in
the partial exemption calculation if the Council does not opt to
tax. Opting to tax would require VAT to be added to rents - this
might be recoverable by the cafe operator and community facility
hirers if they are VAT registered, but it is quite likely that some
smaller groups will not be.
 
Skatepark
Similarly, you need to assess
the VAT treatment of operating income. Will the skatepark itself be
operated by the Council - or will it be let to an operator? I
assume that the commercial kiosk will be a lease/letting,
generating income which will be VAT-exempt unless the Council opts
to tax. As with Walpole Bay, a public toilet operated by the
Council is a non-business activity. Once you have assessed the
proportion of intended exempt activity, determine the effect on
partial exemption, and opt to tax if the de minimis is at
risk.
 
Option To Tax is generally irrevocable for 20 years.
 
Once a property has been opted,
then (apart from a brief "cooling off" period) it cannot normally
be revoked for at least 20 years. However, it currently seems
probable that LGR proposals will result in the creation of a new
unitary authority, which will take on the activities of the
Council, other neighbouring authorities and the relevant parts of
the County. This new authority will likely have a new VAT
registration number. In previous LGR exercises, HMRC have taken the
view that options to tax made by the authorities which cease to
exist under LGR will lapse, and it will be for the successor
authority to decide whether or not it wishes to opt to tax specific
sites. Depending upon both the stage of the works and the successor
authority's forecast of its partial exemption position, it might
decide that it does not need to opt to tax.

Not to opt to tax, this has
been rejected due to advice provided by the Council’s
external VAT advisors and the level of risk associated with
repayment of previously reclaimed VAT.
topline: The Director of Corporate Services & S151 Officer has decided to opt to tax certain regeneration projects to avoid breaching the council's partial exemption limit.

decision_maker: Director of Corporate Services & S151 Officer
content:
Opt to tax the Garlinge
Recreation ground subject to the Home Advantage Programme Project
with effect from 22/07/26 as part of the decision to deliver the
football improvement project on the site.
 
Decision made in agreement with
TDC Surveyor, as we are unable to split out the Community Use
Agreement and works obligation, we will need to follow the advice
to Opt to Tax this property.

This project and all related
documents and proposals were fully reviewed by our tax
consultants.
 
Scope
and Executive Report Received:
 
Garlinge Pavilion and Recreation Grounds – Home Advantage
Programme (HAP)
Thank you for asking PSTAX ("I"
or "we") to provide VAT advice to Thanet District Council ("the
Council) regarding the 25-year lease granted to Ramsgate Football
Club (85) (“the Club”) and the Home Advantage Programme
(HAP) funded works at Garlinge Pavilion and Recreation
Ground.
 
Scope
of the advice
The Council has asked us to
review the peppercorn lease to determine whether the arrangements
constitute a barter transaction and, if so, to assess the
associated VAT treatment.
 
Executive Summary
1. 
The Football Foundation’s Home Advantage
Programme (HAP) requires the Garlinge site to be leased to Ramsgate
FC at a peppercorn rent. However, the current draft lease demands
monetary and non-monetary consideration in the form of insurance
rent and services via the Community Use Agreement (CUA) and
completion of the major structural HAP Works. 
 
2.  Because of these obligations, HMRC will view
this not as a non-business peppercorn arrangement, but a VAT-exempt
business activity
 
3.  If the Council proceeds with the lease as
currently drafted, it creates a barter transaction requiring strict
accounting.
•  The Council must invoice the Club for
the total value of the lease, which is calculated as the insurance
rental costs plus the estimated monetary value of the CUA services
and the HAP works. 
• 
In return, the Club must issue an invoice to the
Council for the same amount for providing CUA and HAP services
(building and pitch improvements).
 
4.  If the Club charges VAT on its invoice, the
Council can only recover this VAT if its total exempt input tax
remains "insignificant" (less than £7,500 per year or 5% of
its total VAT incurred).
 
5.  To minimise irrecoverable VAT costs, the
Council has two options:
 
Option 1: Create a genuine
peppercorn arrangement. The Council must absorb the insurance
costs, remove the CUA and HAP Works obligations from the lease, and
manage them instead through separate agreements. This option is not
possible under the funding requirements.
 
Option 2: The Council could
choose to opt to tax the Garlinge site. The Council would retain
the current lease conditions, including insurance, rental, and
delivery arrangements, for CUA and HAP works. However, the lease
would be subject to standard rate VAT rather than exempt VAT. As a
result, the Council would no longer be subject to partial exemption
restrictions on this site. Opting to tax would mean the Council
must charge the Club VAT at the standard rate on the full lease
consideration.
 
 
Background Information
 
Option To Tax is generally irrevocable for 20 years.
 
Once a property has been opted,
then (apart from a brief "cooling off" period) it cannot normally
be revoked for at least 20 years. However, it currently seems
probable that LGR proposals will result in the creation of a new
unitary authority, which will take on the activities of the
Council, other neighbouring authorities and the relevant parts of
the County. This new authority will likely have a new VAT
registration number. In previous LGR exercises, HMRC have taken the
view that options to tax made by the authorities which cease to
exist under LGR will lapse, and it will be for the successor
authority to decide whether or not it wishes to opt to tax specific
sites.  Depending upon both the stage of
the works and the successor authority's forecast of its partial
exemption position, it might decide that it does not need to opt to
tax.

Not to opt to tax, this has
been rejected due to the implication on the Football Foundation
funding requirements and need to ensure the improvements works are
delivered under lease protections.
topline: The Director of Corporate Services & S151 Officer has decided to opt to tax the Garlinge Recreation ground for the football improvement project.

purpose:
The purpose of this report is
to clarify and codify the schedule of delegation in relation to the
preparation of a local plan. It is considered that these
delegations already lie with the Director of Place. However,
because of significant changes to the statutory plan-making
process, it is considered that it would be beneficial to both
officers and Members to clarify the level of delegated authority
that exists at each stage of plan preparation.
content:
The purpose of this report is
to clarify and codify the schedule of delegation in relation to the
preparation of a local plan. It is considered that these
delegations already lie with the Director of Place. However,
because of significant changes to the statutory plan-making
process, it is considered that it would be beneficial to both
officers and Members to clarify the level of delegated authority
that exists at each stage of plan preparation.

The Leader of Council agreed the delegation
schedule set out at Annex 1 to the decision report.

The schedule provides clarity
on the levels of delegation applied to the process of preparing a
local plan under the new plan-making system, subject to The Town
and Country Planning (Local Planning) (England) Regulations
2026.

The alternative option would be
to rely on the current delegation arrangements. While this is
possible, it is considered that greater clarity on this matter is
beneficial to both officers and members in relation to the local
plan process.
topline: The Leader of the Council has decided to clarify and codify the delegation schedule for the preparation of a local plan

purpose:
To seek formal executive
approval from the Leader of the Council to agree the final
financial terms of sale for the freehold disposal of the former
Pierremont Depot, Broadstairs, following an open market private
treaty disposal process, securing statutory best consideration
under Section 123 of the Local Government Act 1972.
content:
To seek formal executive
approval from the Leader of the Council to agree the final
financial terms of sale for the freehold disposal of the former
Pierremont Depot, Broadstairs, following an open market private
treaty disposal process, securing statutory best consideration
under Section 123 of the Local Government Act 1972.

The Leader agreed the
following:
 
1. 
To agree sales terms for the freehold disposal of
the former Pierremont Depot, Broadstairs (excluding the access
road) to the highest competitive bidder (with a value exceeding
£250,000). 
 
2. 
That authority be delegated to the Director of
Place, in consultation with the Cabinet Member for Regeneration and
Property, to finalise all legal documentation, and execute the land
transfer.

Cabinet agreed to the disposal
of the former depot adjacent to Pierremont Park by way of private
treaty at its meeting held on 25 September 2025.
 
Following this decision, the
council advertised the opportunity and reviewed the submissions
received.
 
Following open market exposure,
the accepted bid represents the highest financial offer obtained.
The terms satisfy Thanet District Council's statutory obligation
under Section 123 of the Local Government Act 1972 to achieve "best
consideration reasonably obtainable".
 
This decision to agree the
final terms of the sale of this property was taken by the Leader of
the Council following consultation with the Cabinet Member for
Regeneration and Property.

Thanet District Council
received two other bids for the site. Both were rejected because
they were significantly less than the highest offer. Although one
was accompanied by a schedule of potential non-monetary benefits
for the council, when these were appraised, they could not be
explicitly quantified in a way that linked back to the
council’s statutory functions and were not sufficiently
robust to justify acceptance of an offer of such significant
undervalue.
topline: The Leader of the Council has decided to sell the former Pierremont Depot in Broadstairs to the highest competitive bidder for a value exceeding £250,000.

content:
Cabinet considered the update
report regarding the UK Shared Prosperity Fund (UKSPF) programme,
which has been instrumental in delivering projects across Thanet
from 2022 to 2026.
 
This report provided a
comprehensive update on our delivery against the three key
investment priorities: Community and Place, Supporting Local
Business, People and Skills. It set out the outcomes achieved
during the extended final phase of the programme (2025-2026),
demonstrating the real-world impact the Council’s
interventions had had in supporting the local economy, boosting
employability, and building pride in the local
communities.
 
The report detailed the
strategic progress made across our diverse project
portfolio—from the successful Youth Employment and Skills
Hub, which was the first of its kind in Kent, to the expansion of
the Teenage Market initiative and the ongoing support provided to
the voluntary and community sector. It also offered a financial
update, confirming that all funding was on track to be fully
utilised by the programme’s conclusion in September 2026.
The report also outlined the steps that
were being taken to sustain these vital initiatives as the Council
looked beyond the current funding cycle.
 
As the Council entered the
final months of this programme, Cabinet was pleased to note the
continued commitment of officers and partners in securing positive
outcomes for Thanet’s residents and businesses, ensuring a
lasting legacy for the work the Council had delivered.
 
Councillor Bayford, Councillor
Pugh and Councillor Austin spoke under Council Procedure Rule
20.1.
 
Councillor Duckworth proposed,
Councillor Albon seconded and Cabinet agreed the
following:
 
1. 
To note the progress and impact achieved in the
delivery of the UK Shared Prosperity programme for
Thanet.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to note the progress and impact achieved in the delivery of the UK Shared Prosperity programme for Thanet.

purpose:
The purpose of this report is
to present the updated Corporate Health & Safety Policy 2026 to
the Cabinet for approval and formal adoption. This overarching
policy governs occupational health and safety across all council
services, reinforcing the council's commitment to providing a safe
working environment for employees, contractors, and the
public.
content:
The purpose of this report is
to present the updated Corporate Health & Safety Policy 2026 to
the Cabinet for approval and formal adoption. This overarching
policy governs occupational health and safety across all council
services, reinforcing the council's commitment to providing a safe
working environment for employees, contractors, and the
public.

Cabinet agreed the
following:
 
1. 
To approve and adopt the Corporate Health &
Safety Policy 2026 (Version 5), replacing the previous November
2023 version, to ensure legal compliance, clear governance, and
continuous performance improvement across all
undertakings.

The prospective decision to
adopt Version 5 of the Corporate Health & Safety Policy is
being made to reformat the framework into the new corporate format
and simplify its content by reducing legislative repetition. It
also moves extensive supplementary documentation to a separate
Annex to keep the core policy focused and manageable, whilst
establishing updated commitments and clear lines of organisational
responsibility.

Do Nothing (Reject the Update).
This was rejected because maintaining Version 4 would leave the
council with outdated corporate formatting and an overly dense
policy structure containing unnecessary legislative text, contrary
to evolving best practices.
topline: The UK council has decided to approve and adopt the Corporate Health & Safety Policy 2026 to ensure legal compliance and continuous performance improvement.

purpose:
The Lifts in the
Council’s Cecil Street offices are over 50 years old and have
reached the end of their effective operational and economic life.
Both lifts consistently break down and repairing them is becoming
impossible because the faulty parts are no longer manufactured.
Cabinet approval was sought to procure a contract for renewing the
passenger lifts.
content:
The Lifts in the
Council’s Cecil Street offices are over 50 years old and have
reached the end of their effective operational and economic life.
Both lifts consistently break down and repairing them is becoming
impossible because the faulty parts are no longer manufactured.
Cabinet approval was sought to procure a contract for renewing the
passenger lifts.

Cabinet agreed the
following:
 
1. 
The key decision to procure and award a contract
with an estimated value of £425,000 to undertake essential
work to renew the lifts, operating equipment and motors, following
a procurement exercise;
 
2. 
That the Director of Place shall negotiate the final
terms and sign the contract with the successful bidder.

1. 
To plan against the risk of failing to meet
statutory requirements under the Equality Act 2010 if the
operational lift becomes defective;
 
2. 
To prevent the potential breach of the Public Sector
Equality Duty (PSED);
 
3. 
To safeguard the long-term utility and desirability
of the Cecil Street offices.

Delay the lift renewal and
continue with reactive, on-demand repair work to the remaining
operational lift.
 
This alternative option was
rejected because it is not a viable long-term solution and could
put the authority at risk of breaching statutory
requirements.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to renew the lifts in the Council's Cecil Street offices to ensure safety and functionality.

purpose:
This report presents the
Council’s Annual Health and Safety Report for the period 1
April 2025 to 30 April 2026. It provides an overview of the
Council’s health and safety performance, highlights key
departmental achievements and challenges, and outlines the
strategic safety priorities for the 2026/2027 period.
content:
This report presents the
Council’s Annual Health and Safety Report for the period 1
April 2025 to 30 April 2026. It provides an overview of the
Council’s health and safety performance, highlights key
departmental achievements and challenges, and outlines the
strategic safety priorities for the 2026/2027 period.

Cabinet agreed the
following:
 
1. 
To approve the updated Corporate Health and Safety
Policy.

The Council holds a legal
obligation under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974 to monitor,
assess, and report on its safety performance. Adopting this report
ensures robust governance, maintains regulatory compliance during
the Local Government Reorganisation, and enables the delivery of
strategic actions intended to transition the authority from a
reactive posture toward a proactive, embedded safety
culture.

Option 2: Reject or defer
approval. This option is rejected as it would leave the Council
operating under outdated policy guidelines, delay critical safety
upgrades, compromise technical compliance, and increase exposure to
regulatory breaches and civil liabilities.
topline: The Council has decided to approve the updated Corporate Health and Safety Policy.

purpose:
This report provides an update
to Cabinet on the disposal of two freehold HRA assets. Cabinet had
previously approved the disposal of the two assets in question and
two additional HRA assets at a meeting held on 16 February
2026.
content:
This report provides an update
to Cabinet on the disposal of two freehold HRA assets. Cabinet had
previously approved the disposal of the two assets in question and
two additional HRA assets at a meeting held on 16 February
2026.

Cabinet agreed the
following:
 
1. 
The Council owned freehold assets at The Leys,
Manston, CT12 5AS and 70-76 Canterbury Road, Birchington, CT7 9BB
are to be disposed of through a direct offer to existing
leaseholders in the first instance and 
if unsuccessful disposed of at public auction.

Following several site visits
by officers and quotes from council-approved contractors for
essential maintenance, it has been determined that the most
effective course of action is to propose the disposal of the two
HRA freehold assets at 70-76 Canterbury Road and The Leys. All of
the flats at both 70-76 Canterbury Road and The Leys are owned by
leaseholders.
 
The recommendation to dispose
was approved at Cabinet on 16 February 2026 and this report seeks
to clarify for Cabinet the disposal procedure and options for the
freeholds.

Option 1 - dispose: This is the
recommendation. To dispose of the council owned freeholds, either
directly or at auction and reinvest the proceeds into the HRA
Capital programme.
 
Option 2 - Retain freehold
interest at 70-76 Canterbury Road and/or The Leys. This would
require the council to perform all obligations that are incumbent
upon freeholders over the long term which would most likely require
further council expenditure and council resources through
commitment of staff time. The income generated through ground rent
at both sites has been considered to not be sufficient to cover the
expected expenditure in the future.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to dispose of two freehold HRA assets owned by the council.

purpose:
This report seeks Cabinet
endorsement for the annual PartnershipOne 2026/27 Business Plan,
marking the second full year of company operations under the Local
Authority Trading Company (LATCo) delivery model.
content:
This report seeks Cabinet
endorsement for the annual PartnershipOne 2026/27 Business Plan,
marking the second full year of company operations under the Local
Authority Trading Company (LATCo) delivery model.

Cabinet approved the PartnershipOne Annual
Business Plan 2026/27.

In-line with established
shareholder governance arrangements, Cabinet is required to approve
the Annual Business Plan to authorise the company's operational
mandate for the financial year.
 
Endorsement ensures that the
company remains strategically aligned with the Council's corporate
priorities while maintaining strict performance management
safeguards over critical public-facing services.

Rejecting or deferring the
Business Plan was considered as an alternative. This option was
rejected because it would disrupt company governance, delay
strategic development, and create operational ambiguity across the
three partner councils
topline: The Council has decided to approve the PartnershipOne Annual Business Plan 2026/27 under the LATCo delivery model.

purpose:
This report provides Cabinet
with a view on the 2025/26 provisional outturn for General Fund
revenue and capital, as well as the Housing Revenue Account (HRA).
It also details how identified structural pressures have informed
the wider Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).
content:
This report provides Cabinet
with a view on the 2025/26 provisional outturn for General Fund
revenue and capital, as well as the Housing Revenue Account (HRA).
It also details how identified structural pressures have informed
the wider Medium-Term Financial Strategy (MTFS).

Cabinet approved the
following:
 
1. 
To endorse the further management controls
implemented to mitigate the anticipated budget shortfall for
2026/27;
 
2. 
The General Fund capital programme budget
adjustments, numbered (i), as set out in section 6.4 of the Cabinet
report.

Management controls are being
further tightened to mitigate the financial pressures from the
2025/26 outturn and the projected service overspend for
2026/27.
 
Capital programme adjustments
are required for the Ramsgate Port - Berth 1 Refurbishment (now
renamed to Ramsgate Port & Harbour Compliance Initiative) to
enable the budget to be used for compliance projects at Ramsgate
Port and Harbour.

Cabinet may have chosen to
approve, alter or reject these recommendations. Rejecting the
recommendations was not chosen as officers would need to report to
Council at a later date on the full implications of doing so and
the necessary mitigation.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to approve management controls and capital programme adjustments to mitigate budget shortfalls and fund compliance projects at Ramsgate Port and Harbour.

purpose:
The council is a Statutory
Harbour Authority with a duty to maintain the Port of Ramsgate and
Ramsgate Royal Harbour. This report proposes the approval of a
contract for Hydrodynamic Dredging (Water Injection Dredging) to
ensure safe navigation. The estimated contract value is
£1,262,500 over a maximum term of 5 years (3 years plus a
2-year extension), funded by an existing recurring revenue
budget.
content:
The council is a Statutory
Harbour Authority with a duty to maintain the Port of Ramsgate and
Ramsgate Royal Harbour. This report proposes the approval of a
contract for Hydrodynamic Dredging (Water Injection Dredging) to
ensure safe navigation. The estimated contract value is
£1,262,500 over a maximum term of 5 years (3 years plus a
2-year extension), funded by an existing recurring revenue
budget.

Cabinet agreed the following,
to:
 
1. 
Approve the key decision to award a contract with a
value in excess of £250,000 for Hydrodynamic Dredging at the
Port of Ramsgate and Ramsgate Royal Harbour, following a
procurement exercise;
 
2. 
Agree that the Director of Environment, having
sought advice from legal services, agree the final terms of any
contract award and sign the contract with the successful
bidder.

The council has a statutory
duty to conserve ports and harbours under its control and to ensure
safe navigation. Regular dredging is required to remove silt
buildup, particularly in the port turning circle and outer harbour.
Failure to dredge would limit the size of craft able to access the
port, reduce revenue, increase operational risk and liability, and
risk breaching the open port duty as defined in the Port Marine
Safety Code.

Reducing the volume of
dredging. This was rejected because it would limit the size of
craft able to access the port, substantially reduce revenue,
increase operational risk and liability regarding vessel
groundings, and increase the risk of breaching the Open Port duty,
exposing the council to legal risk and potential
litigation.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to award a contract for Hydrodynamic Dredging at the Port of Ramsgate and Ramsgate Royal Harbour.

purpose:
To present the Thanet Indoor
Built Sports Facilities Strategy report compiled by an approved
external consultancy, The Sports Consultancy. The strategy provides
an up-to-date audit of supply and demand for indoor sports
provision across the district up to 2040 and proposes strategic
actions to be undertaken between 2026 and 2040.
content:
To present the Thanet Indoor
Built Sports Facilities Strategy report compiled by an approved
external consultancy, The Sports Consultancy. The strategy provides
an up-to-date audit of supply and demand for indoor sports
provision across the district up to 2040 and proposes strategic
actions to be undertaken between 2026 and 2040.

Cabinet agreed the
following:
 
1. 
The formal adoption of the Thanet Indoor Built
Sports Facilities Strategy to shape future sports facility
investment and underpin the emerging Local Plan.

The current indoor built sports
facilities baseline relies on historical data and required updating
in alignment with Sport England's Assessing Needs and Opportunities
Guidance. Adopting the strategy establishes a single, robust
evidence base that enables the Council to attract grant funding,
secure Section 106 developer contributions linked to population
growth, address critical infrastructure deficits (such as an acute
shortage of public water space), and support preventative
healthcare outcomes across Thanet's communities.

Cabinet considered not formally
adopting the Thanet Indoor Built Sports Facilities Strategy and
retaining the previous strategic arrangements. This was rejected
because relying on obsolete facility capacity data limits the
Council's ability to demand Section 106 developer contributions or
access newly established central funding pots, while locking in a
severe decline in public water access by 2040.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to adopt the Thanet Indoor Built Sports Facilities Strategy to shape future sports facility investment and infrastructure development.

purpose:
In

Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) that the UKSPF

At the start of each municipal
year the Leader has to make a decision on whether to re-constitute
any Cabinet Advisory Groups from the previous year in order for
these sub groups to continue to inform policy development by
Cabinet.

To recreate Cabinet Advisory
Groups as per the list set out in the report with the membership
and terms of reference attached at Annexes 1-5.

In the
2025/2026 there were five Cabinet Advisory Groups, these
were:
 
1. 
Local Plan Cabinet Advisory Group
2. 
Housing Cabinet Advisory Group 
3. 
Climate Change Cabinet Advisory
Group 
4. 
Equalities Cabinet Advisory Group 
5. 
Cyber Security Cabinet Advisory
Group 
 
All
five Cabinet Advisory Groups played an important role in the
previous year to review a number of policy initiatives that Cabinet
was actively considering and creating a platform for in-depth
review of various suggestions and proposals in different policy
areas. Continuing with this approach would enhance policy
development and help inform Cabinet decisions and by extension
Council decisions.

The Leader of Council may wish
to create the groups set out in the report, alternatively he may
wish to create some or none at all. This is the officer recommended
approach.
 
The Leader could opt to
discontinue with this approach. However, this approach would lead
to Cabinet missing out on non-Cabinet member contributions to
policy development. And was therefore not recommended.

There
is an ongoing issue of persistent anti-social behaviour (ASB),
rowdy conduct, public intoxication, and public urination/defecation
in the Margate, Broadstairs, and Ramsgate areas. These behaviours
negatively impact local businesses, diminish the visitor
experience, and pose public health risks.
 
Following
the expiration of previous orders and a subsequent pause due to
legal challenges, multi-agency partners have reported increased
difficulty in managing alcohol-related disorder. A statutory
four-week public consultation was carried out between 1 May 2026
and 1 June 2026, receiving overwhelming community and partner
support for the reintroduction of a targeted legal toolbox to
address these issues.

Cabinet
agreed the following:
 
1. 
To give full consideration to the results of
statutory consultation, the results of which are attached at
annexes 12 and 13, in relation to the proposed PSPO;
 
2. 
To consider the evidence base for a PSPO detailed in
the statements attached to this report at Annexes 3,4,5,6 and
7;
 
3. 
To approve the PSPO as drafted and attached to this
report at Annex 1;
 
4. 
That the PSPO shall be implemented with effect from
1 July 2026 in the proposed restricted areas as set out in the maps
which appear within the proposed order attached to this report at
Annex 1.

Statutory Thresholds Met:
Evidence from residents, businesses, and law enforcement confirms
that the detrimental activities are persistent, unreasonable, and
directly damage the community's quality of life.
 
Proportionate Early
Intervention: The PSPO acts as a vital preventative tool, granting
community safety officers and police the legal authority to seize
alcohol or issue Fixed Penalty Notices (£100) before
low-level friction escalates into serious violence.
 
Overwhelming Public Mandate:
The public consultation returned a 96.5% consensus in support of
alcohol restrictions and a 97.58% approval rate for the public
bodily fluids ban. Full, unreserved support was also granted by the
local Chief Inspector of Police and the Kent Police and Crime
Commissioner.

1. 
Relying on Individual Injunctions or CPWs/CPNs:
These alternative enforcement methodologies were rejected because
they are highly resource-intensive, require naming specific
individuals, and fail to efficiently address transient populations
or multi-offender groups. A PSPO correctly attaches to the
geographical space rather than changing faces.
2. 
Altering or Extending the Defined Map Boundaries:
Consultation responses suggested expanding restrictions to areas
like Dane Park or Westgate-on-Sea. These extensions were rejected
at this time because current boundaries match strict evidential
hotspots. However, the framework allows boundaries to be actively
reviewed and modified if displacement patterns justify future
changes.
3. 
Taking No Action: Discounted as it would leave field
teams without the immediate legal powers to confiscate alcohol,
causing further deterioration of public safety, negative trade
margins, and unmanaged public health risks.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to reintroduce a Public Spaces Protection Order in Margate, Broadstairs, and Ramsgate to address persistent anti-social behaviour and public health risks.

Cabinet considered a report seeking approval to migrate the

infrastructure from Google Workspace to Microsoft 365.
The
current contract with Google is due to expire in December 2027 and
cannot be extended due to procurement framework changes.
Additionally, the council must prepare for Local Government
Reorganisation (LGR) which will culminate in the establishment of a
new unitary authority on 1 April 2028. Standardising on Microsoft
365 will align Thanet District Council with all other Kent

preventing integration issues, and mitigating several imminent

content:
Cabinet considered a report seeking approval to migrate the
council's cloud-based productivity, collaboration, and telephony
infrastructure from Google Workspace to Microsoft 365.
The
current contract with Google is due to expire in December 2027 and
cannot be extended due to procurement framework changes.
Additionally, the council must prepare for Local Government
Reorganisation (LGR) which will culminate in the establishment of a
new unitary authority on 1 April 2028. Standardising on Microsoft
365 will align Thanet District Council with all other Kent
authorities (which are already Microsoft-based), ensuring that
staff are equipped with relevant skills ahead of Vesting Day,
preventing integration issues, and mitigating several imminent
licensing cost pressures.

Cabinet
approved the following, to:
 
1. 
Move the organisation from Google workspace to
Microsoft 365. This would include migrating the telephony system
from Google Voice to integrate it within Microsoft
Teams;
 
2. 
Procure a Microsoft 365 tenant during the current
financial year (2026/27). This is on the basis that Microsoft
licences need to be renewed anyway in October 2026. This would run
alongside the current Google Workspace environment until the Google
contract ends in December 2027;
 
3. 
Retain Gemini as the organisation’s preferred
AI platform rather than purchasing Co-pilot licenses.

Operational collaboration and
alignment: Moving to Microsoft 365 eliminates operational barriers
and technical workarounds currently required to collaborate with
central government, neighbouring councils, and other
Microsoft-based external partners.
 
Local Government Reorganisation
(LGR) preparedness: Standardising on Microsoft 365 aligns Thanet
with all other Kent councils ahead of the transition to a new
unitary authority on 1 April 2028. This minimises potential
operational disruption for staff on Vesting Day and allows
sufficient training time.
 
Addressing licence cost
pressures: The council's current standalone Microsoft Office
Standard 2021 licences expire in October 2026. Transitioning to
Microsoft 365 removes an immediate pressure of £259,000 that
would otherwise be required to renew these standalone
licences.
 
Enhanced security and device
management: The Microsoft ecosystem enables improved mobile device
management and cybersecurity features through Intune and Autopilot,
aligning with the council's recent rollout of Windows laptops and
mitigating key corporate risks.
 
Cost-effective AI utilisation:
Retaining Gemini AI is more financially viable than purchasing 500
Microsoft Co-pilot licences, which would add an unbudgeted
£138,600 annual revenue pressure. Gemini is a highly praised
tool that staff are already trained and comfortable
using.

Do nothing: Rejected because
the current Google Workspace contract expires in December 2027 and
cannot be extended under the former G-Cloud 13 procurement
framework.
 
Decline migration and procure a
new Google Workspace contract in late 2027: This was rejected for
several critical reasons.
 
Financial risk: Future
short-term Google contract costs are unknown and technology
industry pricing generally is highly volatile; additionally, the
council would still face the immediate £259,000 cost pressure
in October 2026 to renew standalone Microsoft licences.
 
Strategic isolation: Thanet
would remain an outlier as the only Kent authority on Google,
limiting joint working and missing a crucial upskilling window for
staff ahead of the LGR transition in April 2028. This would result
in much higher disruption when the new unitary council begins, as
the new council is extremely likely to adopt Microsoft.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to migrate Thanet District Council's cloud-based infrastructure from Google Workspace to Microsoft 365.

purpose:
The purpose of this report is
to establish a comprehensive delivery plan for the national Crisis
and Resilience Fund monies distributed to Thanet District Council
(CRF).
content:
The purpose of this report is
to establish a comprehensive delivery plan for the national Crisis
and Resilience Fund monies distributed to Thanet District Council
(CRF).

Cabinet
agreed the following, to:
 
1. 
Approve the adoption of the ‘Phased hybrid
model’ (Option 3) to manage the Crisis and Resilience Fund
over its three-year lifecycle;
 
2. 
Note that by approving Option 3;
 
The
budget is as follows:
 

For Year 1
Delivery partners - £181,000
ColdBusters - £181,000
CRF
Community coordination - £60,000;
Administrative costs - £30,000
Total -
£452,000
 
For
both Year 2 and 3 we
anticipate:
ColdBusters - £292,000
CRF
Community coordination -£100,000
Administrative costs - £60,000
Total -
£452,000;
 
3.  Delegate authority to the
Head of Housing and Planning to make minor amendments to the
proposed allocation of funding, in consultation with the Cabinet
member for housing, if any questions arise during the delivery
phase of the scheme.

The primary reasons for this
decision include:
Thanet District Council must
establish a comprehensive delivery plan for the newly introduced
national Crisis and Resilience Fund (CRF). Kent County Council
(KCC) holds the main part of the fund, 20% of KCC total funds have
been disturbed to district councils, of which Thanet for Year 1 has
received £451,874.71.
 
Four options have been
considered for how Thanet District Council can deliver the funding.
Senior officers of the Council have debated these and option 3 is
the recommended delivery model. The full options (for transparency)
are set out in the report.

Reject
the funds from KCC - this is not recommended given the acute need
that exists in Thanet and the proven ability of the Council and its
funding partners to deliver schemes such as the Household Support
Fund and do tremendous good with it.
 
Full
partner delivery - While this model can be implemented more
quickly, adopting it significantly reduces Thanet District
Council’s direct control over spend priorities. There is a
specific risk that delivery partners may default to prioritising
social housing tenants as they get a higher percentage of the funds
making the fund difficult to access for private renters or
residents in the private sector. This would leave the Council open
to scrutiny and issues with the funding if this approach was
adopted for three years. It may also place an administrative strain
on delivery partners for whom this burden will be
higher.
 
Full
direct Council delivery - While there are a number of positive
attributes to this option, such as enabling the Council to align
its distribution with the district’s deep pockets of
deprivation and unlocking the Coldbusters scheme outlined above,
the Council would not have a full year to deliver this funding in
Year 1 (with funding needing to be spent by 31st March 2027). There
is a high administrative and data-tracking burden for this scheme
though an administrative role would be able to absorb this.
Following on from this it would also require immediate, rapid
recruitment (ECFs, internal approvals and potentially notice
periods to be worked etc) within a tight operational window for the
first part of Year 1. This would make it very difficult to deliver
all funds in Year 1. Failure to do so could limit the amount of
funding the Council receives for year 2 and 3 delivery.
 
Split
funding model - While this spreads the risk and enables the Council
to work with delivery partners still, splitting the budget dilutes
the scaling power of the total fund. 
 
Increase crisis grants and reduce the ColdBusters focus - This
would create significant overlap with the huge countywide crisis
scheme already being managed by KCC, making it an inefficient use
of Thanet’s local fund compared to the Cold Busters scheme
which builds long-term household resilience and supports those
uniquely in crisis. This option is not recommended.
topline: The Cabinet has decided to adopt a 'Phased hybrid model' to manage the Crisis and Resilience Fund distributed to Thanet District Council, with specific budget allocations for delivery partners, ColdBusters, and administrative costs.
